resources.string: Calibration

Nine short blocks, about nine minutes. You will do nothing, read, and then something deliberately hard. The app compares your brain activity across the three to learn what concentrating looks like for you.

Keep your eyes open the whole time, including the easy blocks — closing them changes the signal far more than concentrating does, and would make the result meaningless. Sit still, and stay off your phone apart from the tasks.

The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of the same name in 1901, and for half a century nobody could say what it was. The corroded bronze fragments held gear teeth cut to a precision that would not be seen again for well over a thousand years. X-ray imaging in the 1970s, and computed tomography in 2005, eventually settled the question: it was an astronomical calculator. Turning a handle on the side advanced the date, and pointers on the faces moved to show the positions of the sun and moon, the phase of the moon, and the timing of eclipses. One dial tracked the four-year cycle of athletic games. The device encoded the irregular motion of the moon through a pin-and-slot arrangement between two gears mounted slightly off-centre, which produced a varying speed from a constant input. Nothing else of comparable complexity survives from the ancient world, and no text describes it directly.
What did turning the handle on the side of the mechanism do?
Advanced the date and moved the astronomical pointers
Wound a spring that drove the device for a day
Selected which of the four-year games to display

For most of the twentieth century it was assumed that stomach ulcers were caused by stress and excess acid, and treated accordingly, with bland diets and acid suppression that relieved symptoms without curing anything. In 1982 two researchers in Perth, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, proposed that a spiral bacterium living in the stomach lining was responsible. The claim was poorly received: the stomach was held to be far too acidic for bacteria to survive. Unable to infect an animal model and frustrated by the slow pace of review, Marshall drank a culture of the organism himself. He developed gastritis within days, and a biopsy confirmed the bacterium had colonised his stomach. The pair received the Nobel Prize in 2005. The condition is now routinely cured with a course of antibiotics.
Why did Marshall drink the bacterial culture?
He could not infect an animal model and review was slow
He wanted to prove the stomach was not acidic
It was the standard test for gastritis at the time

Venice is built on millions of wooden piles driven into the silt of the lagoon. Alder, larch and oak were floated down from the forests of Slovenia and Croatia, sharpened, and hammered through the soft upper mud until they met a denser layer of compacted clay beneath. The buildings do not rest on the wood so much as on that clay, with the piles acting as a way of reaching it. The timber has survived for centuries because it sits permanently below the waterline, where there is almost no oxygen, and the organisms that rot wood cannot work. Minerals carried by the water have gradually infiltrated the grain, leaving the piles harder than when they were driven. The threat to the city has never been the foundations; it is the rising water above them.
Why has the timber under Venice not rotted?
It sits below the waterline where there is almost no oxygen
The species used are naturally resistant to decay
It was treated with minerals before being driven
